newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Obscure soldiers seize power in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: Obscure soldiers seize power in Sierra Leone.

text.p: Soldiers seized power in Sierra Leone in a new twist to the troubles of the West African state whose mining-based economy was shattered by civil war.
A corporal announced Sunday's coup toppling the one-year-old elected government of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who fled by helicopter to neighbouring Guinea.
Radio statements made by coup spokesmen gave no substantive clue about the real powers behind the takeover.
But one of the first decrees they announced reflected grievances in the army against Kabbah, who took over in March 1996 from military rulers who had taken power four years earlier.
The decree abolished a civilian militia force on which Kabbah had come to rely to combat rebels in continuing fighting despite an accord last year ending five years of civil war.
At the start of the coup, soldiers stormed Freetown's maximum security prison and freed some 600 inmates including soldiers charged with plotting against Kabbah.

Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United States, John Leigh, told CNN that the soldiers distributted arms and ammunition to their jailed colleagues and common criminals who joined later attacks on government buildings.

He described the coup as a setback to democracy and to international efforts to rebuild his country after the civil war. "This is totally surprising and totally uncalled for. There is no need for a coup in Sierra Leone today," Leigh said in Washington.

"Now Sierra Leone is going to be in a difficult condition...All the aid and and all the job I have been doing over here to bring economic development to Sierra Leone are now on hold until this matter is resolved."
State radio announced late on Sunday that the country's land borders and air and sea ports were closed until further notice.
The capital Freetown spent its first night under a night curfew imposed after widespread looting of Lebanese-owned businesses, private homes and United Nations offices and residences.
Hospital sources said at least five civilians were killed and several people, both soldiers and civilians, were wounded in a day of sustained machinegun, mortar and rocket-propelled grenade fire.
Soldiers involved in the coup fought gunbattles with Nigerian troops stationed in Sierra Leone under regional defence pacts.
Nigerian and Guinean troops had supported the government army against rebels, but the radio said all foreign troops had been ordered to return to base until further notice.

The United States embassy was hit twice by rocket fire, prompting Washington to order its citizens in Freetown to stay indoors. No one was injured but a White House spokesman said plans were ready for the evacuation of U.S. nationals if necessary.

"We have advised U.S. citizens in Sierra Leone to stay indoors and we've made preparations in the event that there needs to be an evacuation, but there is no evacutation going on at this point," White House spokesman Barry Toiv said.
A coup spokesman, identified as Corporal Gborie, said in a radio broadcast that junior ranks had toppled Kabbah and asked Nigerian troops not to intervene in what he called an internal matter.
One official said Nigerian troops had tried to prevent the Sierra Leone soldiers entering certain areas.
Small-arms fire and the occasional crash of mortar shells continued into Sunday afternoon and a government building near State House in Freetown was set ablaze.
